# On the Strange Gift of Attention in a Distracted Age

There's a peculiar magic that happens when you really watch something. Not the hurried glance we give to most of the world, but actual watching—the kind where your attention settles on a single point like a bird landing on a branch, and everything else falls away. I've been thinking about this a lot lately, particularly about how rare this experience has become, and how desperately we seem to need it.

Last week I watched a spider build a web. I didn't mean to—I was sitting on my porch with coffee, supposed to be checking emails on my phone, but the spider caught my eye. It was one of those garden spiders, yellow and black, methodical and unhurried. I set the phone down and just watched. For fifteen minutes, maybe twenty. I lost track of time in a way I almost never do anymore.

The spider worked in a spiral pattern, starting from the center and moving outward. Each leg moved with precise coordination, affixing the silk to anchor points on the fence and the porch railing. There was nothing particularly unusual happening—it was just a spider doing what spiders do. But somewhere in watching it, I felt something untangle in my chest. A kind of settling. A reminder that there was a world that operated according to its own logic, independent of my anxieties, my to-do lists, my half-formed worries about the future.

I wonder how many hours I've lost to distraction without even realizing it was happening. Not lost, exactly—that implies I had it and it was taken from me. Rather, hours I never quite possessed in the first place because my attention was scattered across fifteen different places simultaneously. I think about all the moments I've half-experienced: the meal I ate while working, the conversation I had while mentally composing an email, the sunset I photographed instead of watched.

There's this feeling I get sometimes, usually late at night, that I'm living my life in fast-forward, always moving to the next thing, the next notification, the next piece of information. And the peculiar irony is that all this access to more information, more connections, more entertainment than any human in history has ever had—it's somehow made us lonelier and more scattered. We're drowning in stimulation while starving for attention.

I've started noticing how differently people behave when they've actually decided to pay attention to something. There's a quality to their presence that changes. You can see it in someone's eyes when they're really listening versus when they're just waiting for their turn to talk. You can see it in how differently people draw when they're actually looking at what they're drawing versus working from memory. The results are night and day.

Children are like this naturally, before we train it out of them. I watched my nephew play with a cardboard box for an hour last month. Not a toy—a box. But in his mind, it was a spaceship, a fort, a mountain range, a car, a house. He was completely absorbed, moving between these different narratives with total commitment. His attention wasn't divided; it was fully deployed to this single object and the worlds he was constructing around it. And the remarkable thing was how calm he was. How content. There was no sense of missing out on something better that might be happening elsewhere.

Somewhere along the line, we've been convinced that attention is a commodity to be spent efficiently, that we should be multitasking, that the ability to rapidly shift focus between multiple streams of information is a virtue. Silicon Valley engineers have basically weaponized the human attention span, designing systems specifically to fracture our focus and keep us in a constant state of low-level arousal. Every notification, every red badge, every autoplay feature is a small hook designed to pull our attention away from whatever we're doing.

And the strange part is that we've internalized this. We've begun to feel like something is wrong if we're not feeling that constant pull, that constant stimulation. Boredom has become almost dangerous in our conception—a void that must be immediately filled. We've lost the ability to let our minds wander, to sit with our own thoughts, to experience the kind of deep focus that used to be the default state of human consciousness.

I read somewhere that the average person's attention span has decreased significantly in the last two decades. We're supposedly down to something like eight seconds before we need a new stimulus. That's less than a goldfish, the article said, as if we'd become somehow less intelligent, less capable than a fish. But I don't think that's quite right. It's not that we've become less capable of attention—it's that we've collectively decided to outsource that function to devices that are explicitly designed to prevent us from sustaining it.

What strikes me most is that we know this isn't making us happier. The data is pretty clear on this. More screen time correlates with increased anxiety, depression, and loneliness. More options correlates with more decision paralysis and less satisfaction. More information doesn't correlate with better decision-making. Yet we keep running toward these things, convinced that the next update, the next feature, the next notification will be the one that finally satisfies us.

There's something almost religious about the way we relate to our devices now. We check them first thing in the morning and last thing at night. We look at them when we're uncomfortable or anxious—not to solve anything, just to feel less alone with our thoughts. We photograph our experiences instead of living them, curating our lives for an invisible audience. We've built a whole secondary existence on screens, and increasingly, it feels more real and more important than the primary one.

But here's what I've started to notice: the moments that actually matter to me—the moments I think about later, that change something in how I see the world—those are almost always moments of genuine attention. Not the curated, carefully photographed moments. The messy, unfiltered ones where I was just present. The conversation with a friend where we actually got vulnerable. The moment I realized how my parent's hands had aged. The time I got lost in a city and had to actually look at where I was instead of following GPS. The spider building its web.

I think we're all starving for this but we don't quite know how to say it. We feel it as a vague dissatisfaction, a sense that something is missing. We try to fill it with more information, more entertainment, more connection through screens, but those things don't actually address the hunger. The hunger is for presence. For realness. For the experience of giving something our full attention and being changed by it.

There's a line in a poem I love by Mary Oliver: "Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?" And I think about that whenever I catch myself reflexively reaching for my phone, and I think: not this. Not this scattered, half-present version of living. Not this constant reaching for the next thing while missing the current one.

I don't think the solution is to become a luddite or to completely unplug—that's not realistic for most of us, and honestly, technology has genuine benefits. But I think we need to become more intentional about where our attention goes. We need to treat it as the precious and finite resource it actually is.

I've been trying to practice something small: one thing at a time. Actually, fully, completely one thing at a time. When I eat, I eat. When I listen, I listen. When I work, I work. Not in a manic, focused way, but in a natural, absorbing way. And the strange thing is, when I actually do this, everything gets better. Work is more productive because I'm not divided. Relationships are deeper because the other person can feel that they have my full attention. Meals taste better. Walks are more interesting. The world becomes more vivid.

I think this is what people mean when they talk about mindfulness, though that word has been so commercialized and packaged that it's almost lost its meaning. But really, it's just this: paying attention. To what's actually happening, to what's actually in front of you, right now, in this moment. Because that's all we ever really have. Not our memories of the past or our fears about the future, but this present moment. And when we're not fully in it, we're essentially not fully living.

The spider finished its web as the sun was setting. The whole structure was suddenly visible as the light hit it at an angle, each strand catching the gold of the evening. It was beautiful in a way that a photograph couldn't quite capture. And I thought about how many webs get built every day that no one watches, how many small, intricate moments happen around us completely unwitnessed. I thought about how much beauty I've probably missed by not paying attention.

I don't know if I'll ever be able to completely break free from the fractured attention that our devices demand. But I'm starting to believe that even small moments of real, complete attention are transformative. That reclaiming the ability to focus deeply, to watch patiently, to be truly present—this might be one of the most important things we can do for ourselves and for each other.

So maybe start small. Watch something. Really watch it. A spider, a bird, a person you love. Notice what happens when you let your attention settle, when you stop trying to multitask and just let yourself be in one place, with one thing, fully. It's harder than you'd think in our current moment. But I promise it's worth it.
